fields.description: Make hook-fired writes, such as session registration, events and task status changes, always target the real database even inside a sandboxed worktree.
fields.context: After E-1426 retired companion files, the sessions table is ground truth for Claude-pane registration.
fields.analysis:
## Known limitation: deferred to E-1458 (2026-05-23)

E-1450's "all hook-fired writes go to the real DB" rule is correct for production but unconditional — it leaves no affordance for legitimate self_dev testing scenarios where a developer wants to exercise the hook binaries (the 5-10 separate Go apps per E-893 / E-1367 fan-out) against a sandbox DB without polluting the real ledger.

Implement E-1450 as designed. The current edge-case carve-outs in the prompt (test-fixture detection, sandbox-init bypass) are stand-ins, not a full solution. When hook testing against the sandbox becomes a felt need, **E-1458** ("Allow opt-in hook routing to sandbox DB for self_dev testing") addresses it properly — an opt-in mechanism (env var, per-event marker, or wrapper) that bypasses the IsSandboxActive() override at the hook entry.

Until E-1458 lands, hook tests must either inject DB handles explicitly or accept that hook events leak to the real DB.

## From the description

Fix: ALL hook-fired writes (session registration, event emission, task-status transitions) target the real DB regardless of sandbox routing,

because these reflect real-world activity not test fixture data.

Rare edge cases can be carved out individually.

fields.context: Feeds the You/Agent split and the Goal line in session next.
fields.analysis:
Session-next accuracy finding (session 504 investigation, 2026-05-27): session_tasks records ANY task touched under a session_id, agent or human, including incidental grooming. Example: E-999/E-1064/E-1073 were recorded against session 504 because that session (the agent, acting on Mike's behalf) ran task-update on them. Accurate history, but not 'what the session worked on'. So the relation column must let session-next separate goal/surfaced/revisited work from incidental edits, and the render-side terminal-status filter (per E-1421) must drop completed/confirmed touches from the Remaining view.

Actor-identity (OPEN QUESTION -- discuss when working E-1462; not yet decided, do not pre-frame as multiple-choice): actor.id is currently built as USER@hostname (event_bridge.py emit_event, ~line 68), e.g. mikeschinkel@m4macmini.local, and is identical for agent- and human-run CLI, so the two are indistinguishable at the actor level. The current user@machine form carries useful provenance (who AND which machine) worth preserving -- do NOT collapse it to a bare 'claude'/'user'. Candidate to discuss: keep user@machine but prefix it with a role, e.g. agent:claude@m4macmini.local vs user:mikeschinkel@m4macmini.local. That distinguishes agent from human, keeps machine provenance, and generalizes to multi-user (future scope). Open sub-questions: the role vocabulary (agent/user vs claude/human), how agent context is detected (e.g. the CLAUDECODE env var Claude Code injects), and whether the role lives in actor.id or a separate actor field. Caveat: distinguishing agent from human filters human-CLI pollution but would NOT exclude E-999/1064/1073 (agent grooming, so role would be 'agent'); the relation column plus terminal-status filter are what handle incidental-vs-goal.

fields.analysis:
## session status: the sweep must not drop the ownership signal

Noted 2026-09-11 from E-2111's session, which hit the failure this prevents.

`session status` exposes `--json` and no text flag, so this sweep is what gives
it an agent-facing view at all. That view has a requirement the other commands
do not: **who owns each row is carried by a GLYPH, and only by a glyph.**

`classify()` in `internal/sessionstatuscmd` tests `IsFocal` before `InFlight`,
so a row renders `●` when it is this session's own task and `⟳` when a
non-focal row is in flight — meaning another session is working it. That single
character is the whole signal. The JSON already carries it structurally as
`is_focal`, `in_flight` and `relation`; the text view must carry an equivalent
in words.

WHY THIS MATTERS. A session that cannot tell its own work from another
session's reports the other session's work back to the user, who then receives
the same item twice — once here and once from the session that actually owns it.
That happened: a `/whats-left` report told Mike to confirm E-2128 and to spawn
E-1881, both of which belonged to ES-1199. The glyph was on screen and was
misread. In a text view where the glyph is simply gone, it is not misreadable,
it is unavailable.

Concretely, the agent view of a row needs enough to answer "is this mine?" —
`relation` (claimed vs surfaced) and `in_flight` at minimum. The owning session
id is NOT needed for the render: a user navigates to a session by task id, and
an agent only needs to know the row is not its own. `--json` may carry the id
even though the text view does not.

This is also the clearest evidence for `--agent` over `--plain`. Rendering
"another session is working this" where the human view prints `⟳` is not
stripping chrome; it is rendering for a reader who cannot interpret a glyph.

## From the description

Scope is the FLAG SURFACE only: rename --llm to --agent on the 12 commands carrying both flags, remove --llm rather than keeping a deprecated alias per no-legacy, add --format wherever an output flag exists, and add --json to task deps and task relations, the two commands having --llm and no --json.

Rejected --plain, which this task originally proposed on the premise that the flag merely strips chrome from human output: it does not.

task show --llm emits key=value lines with fields regrouped and relations flattened, so --plain would misname it in the opposite direction from --llm; --agent names what actually varies, the reader.

Explicitly NOT in scope: writing agent renderings for the 16 commands that have --json and no agent view.

fields.description: Fix just land so recording the landing runs in a fresh process after the merge, instead of failing when the landed branch changed the event bridge or config code it loads.
fields.notes:
E-1474 makes it recoverable; this task prevents it on the canonical 'just land' path.

fields.context: Observed 2026-05-29 landing E-1510 (which added config.resolved_worktree_endless_go).
fields.analysis:
Recurred 2026-08-20 landing E-2011, which renamed endless.project_path.normalize
to resolved: main advanced, `_record_landing`'s lazy `from endless.event_bridge
import emit_event` loaded post-merge code against the pre-merge
endless.project_path still in sys.modules, and the land died with `cannot import
name 'resolved' from 'endless.project_path'`. No task_landings row; re-running
`just land` recorded it. Same function, same import, same mechanism as the
2026-05-29 occurrence on E-1510. Filed again as E-2013 before this task was
found; E-2013 is declined as a duplicate and carries a plan whose design is the
in-product fork this task's sibling E-1516 objects to.

Two things have changed since this was filed, and both bear on the chosen remedy.

1. It now fires on the CANONICAL path, not the bare one. The `just land` recipe
   makes a single `endless worktree land` call — E-1941 deliberately moved the
   schema-apply step OUT of the Justfile and INTO the command, so that the apply
   happens after the ff-merge. So the single-process path this task treats as
   "the canonical path fixed by Justfile orchestration" is the only path there
   is, and E-1516's stated promotion trigger ("if the bare path becomes more
   commonly used") has effectively fired.

2. The `--no-record` / `--record-only` split under-covers. It isolates Step 6
   only. Everything E-1941 and E-1799/E-1800 have since moved after the ff-merge
   runs in that same exposed process: `_apply_branch_schema_changes` (5.5),
   `_run_post_land_script`, `_check_post_land_residue`, `_reap_stale_worktrees`.
   Whichever of them imports a module for the first time after the merge is
   equally exposed, and which one that is depends on what the process happened to
   touch earlier — so the failure is order-dependent and will not reproduce.
   The loud case is an ImportError; the quiet case is a newly-imported module
   reading an already-cached module's changed constant, which raises nothing.

Consequence for the decision this task is blocked on: the Justfile-is-the-dev-only
-layer escape hatch got narrower when E-1941 moved work inward. Isolating the
whole post-merge tail — not just the recording — is what the fix has to do,
whether it is done by the recipe or inside the command.

## From the description

Fix: add --no-record flag to 'endless worktree land' (inverse of E-1479's --record-only); update the just land recipe to call 'endless worktree land --no-record E-N' then 'endless worktree land --record-only E-N'.

The second invocation is a fresh Python process — consistent imports.

Bare 'endless worktree land' (no Justfile) still has the bug along that path; a separate maybe task tracks whether to address it.

fields.title: Add a table for typed task content
fields.description: Add a task content table so a task can hold many typed content items such as outcome, notes, analysis and justification, replacing the fixed content columns.
fields.notes: Discussed in a recent session that I cannot relocate; surfaced again 2026-06-05 during epic-type design — Mike flagged it as the better long-term shape for epic narrative storage and as the storage location for type=research justification text.
fields.analysis:
Per ED-1509 (epic content-field convention): once this table exists, revisit epic content storage with purpose-specific content types instead of overloading the legacy columns — in particular a 'design' content type for an epic's design/decisions/interface-contracts (currently overloaded into 'analysis'), and possibly distinct 'vision' and 'roadmap' types. Choose types for fit-for-purpose, not by reusing the few existing columns. ED-1509's field semantics are storage-agnostic and survive this migration.


## Scope split settled 2026-09-13: ship the TABLE, defer the POLICY

The reason this has been deferred is the design space it opens: once content is
not constrained to a fixed set of columns, do content names change per task
type, and are names added or removed for specific types? That question is real
and it is large.

It is also SEPARABLE, and separating it is what makes this task shippable.

- **The table is a storage change.** Ship `task_content` carrying exactly today's
  four names with today's semantics, and behaviour is unchanged.
- **The vocabulary is a policy change.** Whether a brainstorm gets `findings`
  instead of `plan` needs no answer for the table to land.

In a row store, adding a name later is an INSERT, not a migration. That is the
entire point of the change — and it means DEFERRING this task is the expensive
option, because until it lands every new content need costs a column.

Corollary Mike raised and worth holding: this will never be one-and-done. New
content kinds get identified on an ongoing basis. So what is settled once is the
CONVENTION, not the list — one lowercase single-token name per content kind, and
the same token used by `task_content.name`, the Agent Folio Format `Name` header,
and the CLI flag. A new content kind then inherits the rule without a fresh
decision, and no mapping between vocabularies is ever needed.

## NOT blocked by E-894

An earlier framing in discussion claimed this needed a working ledger rebuild,
and therefore the Go port first. That was wrong and is withdrawn.

What this actually needs is the PROJECTOR taught to write `task_content` rows,
plus an ordinary SQLite migration moving existing column values into rows.
Rebuild is the disaster-recovery path, not the deploy path. The only true
residual is that rebuild — already broken, and on hold until after E-894 — gains
one more thing it must learn whenever it is fixed. That is not a prerequisite.

## Relationship to the agent-output work

This makes `task meta` cheaper rather than harder. `meta` reports which content
fields exist and how large they are; over columns that is computed per field,
over `task_content` it is one query returning exactly that shape.

It is also where decision content lands if E-1868 proceeds — see E-1861's
analysis for the two-homes split (`tasks.type='decision'` for architectural
decisions, a `decision` content row for implementation decisions) and for why a
decision needs parts rather than one capped description field.



## A first import for this table (noted by E-2155, 2026-09-18)

E-2155's refusal inventory is 1136 rows — one per user-facing refusal or warning
site, with its class, remedy or decision, and notes. It is committed as a TSV
under docs/ because E-2159 reads it row by row while converting, and because
nothing in Endless stores tabular research today.

That file is the exception this table removes. When task_content ships, import
those rows as typed content on E-2155 and delete the file: it is per-task,
typed, and machine-read, which is exactly the shape this table is for. Worth
checking against the schema while designing it — a 1136-row set is a useful
stress case for whether content rows are one-per-artifact or one-per-record.




## Surface words are a per-type display concern, not a second stored name

Folded down from E-1992 when that task became an epic, because the convention
this task already settled is what governs it.

The primary instruction content stays ONE stored name. The word varies only at
the surface, where agents read and write it: `--plan` on todo/bugfix/epic,
`--brief` on research, `--topic` on brainstorm, rendering under the matching
heading. `--plan` stays accepted on every task type as a universal alias, so an
agent reaching for it on a brainstorm lands in the right row instead of an
error.

Storage stays singular because the objection being answered is behavioural — an
agent resists "plan" on a brainstorm — and behaviour is driven by the flag and
the label, not by the schema. Singular storage also keeps the plan-present gate
one question with no per-type mapping behind it.

This sits with the deferred vocabulary policy above, not with the table: the
table ships carrying today's names, and nothing here has to be answered first.

fields.title: Add endless epic status command
fields.description: Add 'endless epic status <id>', a dashboard for one epic showing its state, every child's phase, status, blockers and session, and which children are actionable next.
fields.analysis:
# Design reasoning — epic status vs session status

## Decision (2026-06-29, Mike)

Chose (a) + (c): **keep `epic status`, re-scoped to not duplicate `session status`,
but defer it** (phase `later`) until a concrete coordinator need arises that
`session status` cannot meet. Surfaced while coordinating E-1537 by hand with
`epic list` / `epic show` / `task bind`.

## The two reads are a "status family" — same presentation, different anchor

`session status` / `session monitor` (the soon-to-be-renamed `session next`, E-1465)
is **session-anchored, bottom-up**: it resolves a *focal task* from the current tmux
window (live session active-task → `@endless_task_id` → most-recent live session) and
shows that task's neighborhood — parent/spawning task, siblings worked by other
sessions on the same focal, cross-session in-flight work, and the focal's direct
dependents. Its row set is driven by which sessions are live and the dependency graph
around the focal. Answers: "what's happening across the swarm around the work I'm on."

`epic status` is **epic-anchored, top-down**: given an explicit epic id, it shows the
epic's own state plus the COMPLETE roster of its children. Answers: "what's the full
state of epic E-NNN so I can decide what to spawn or unblock next."

## Why session status does NOT subsume epic status

Three structural gaps session status can't close:

1. **Targeting any epic from anywhere, no session required.** session status can only
   reach an epic if you're in a session whose focal *is* that epic. epic status takes an
   id — works from a plain shell, for an epic with zero live sessions, for an epic you're
   not currently working in. For a coordinator this is the common case, not the edge.
2. **The complete roster, including what's not moving.** session status's children come
   from live sessions + the focal's graph neighbors, so a not-started / blocked /
   session-less child can be absent. A coordinator's job is exactly seeing those — the
   "what's left."
3. **Next-actionable hint** (ready children, no open blockers) is an epic-roster
   computation, not a session-neighborhood one.

It also must earn its place against `epic show --children` (E-1540), which already prints
a static children table. epic status's differentiator over both siblings: roster +
*live* decorations (blocker / active-session per child) + actionability, targetable by id.

## Scope cut

- IN: epic's own state; complete child roster (every child) with phase, status, blocker
  indicator, active-session indicator; next-actionable hint. Reuse the decoration layer
  `session next` already computes in Go (blocked-by/blocks, active-session) — don't
  re-derive.
- OUT: cross-session in-flight / parent-spawn neighborhood (that's session status's job at
  the keyboard); full child descriptions / plan text / decision history (that's epic show
  / task show).

## Deferral

Committed but parked at `later`: build it when the coordinator need bites and session
status demonstrably can't cover it. The implementation plan is intentionally NOT written
yet — author it at pickup. Was blocked by E-1540 (the `epic` command group), now satisfied
(E-1540 assumed).

## From the description

Shows the epic's own state plus the COMPLETE child roster (every child, including not-started/blocked/session-less ones) with per-child phase, status, blocker indicator, and active-session indicator, plus a 'next actionable' hint (ready children, no open blockers). Built on the decoration layer 'session next' already computes in Go (reuse, don't re-derive).

Explicitly does NOT reproduce session status's cross-session in-flight / parent-spawn neighborhood (that's session status's job at the keyboard), nor epic show's child descriptions/plan text.

Unique value = explicit-id targeting + complete roster + actionability.

fields.analysis:
# Verification-suite system — design analysis

Per ED-1509, this epic's `analysis` holds the distilled design (vision, locked decisions,
interface contracts); the forward roadmap is in the epic's plan (`--text`); the full research is
in E-1600's `outcome`.

## Vision

A product feature of Endless: every task that reaches `verify` carries a committed, executable
**verification suite** — the complete test set (unit + end-to-end) proving that task's
acceptance criteria. Runnable three ways: (a) a bare `git clone` with Endless NOT installed;
(b) `endless verify <id>` on the user's behalf; (c) an AI agent so the user needn't run it.

## Terminology

- **verification suite** — the committed, executable proof of a task's acceptance criteria
  (unit + e2e). (Avoids "artifact," which in CI/CD means a build output.)
- **test runner** — the execution engine that runs the suite (`go test`, `pytest`, `bats`,
  testscript). Endless is never the test runner; it discovers suites, invokes the runner,
  isolates the run, normalizes results, presents pass/fail. (Avoids "runtime.")

## Load-bearing constraint

Endless must require NO external tool to use the core feature. Requiring mise/Docker/etc. would
itself be a reason not to adopt Endless. Heavier tooling must never become a precondition; the
design only must not block adding it later.

## Design principles

1. Triple-runnable (bare clone with no Endless / by Endless / by an agent).
2. Discoverer/orchestrator, never the test runner — convention + manifest, not a dependency.
3. Native runners underneath + a uniform discovery/result contract on top.
4. The suite is ALL testing for the task's scope (unit + e2e); may be slow when needed. Tiering
   = when you run (smoke vs full), not what's included.
5. CLI-only is a PRO — lets Endless drive tools invisibly.
6. All-Go future: no Python/uv lock-in.
7. Not a CI/CD platform. Hermetic builds / production parity are user-owned.
8. The chosen form must be trivially authorable by an AI agent with minimal-to-zero user input.

## Locked decisions (2026-06-20, post E-1600 research)

1. **Result contract = CTRF schema, subset implementation, vendored writer.** Implement only the
   CTRF fields we need, field-names/shapes matching CTRF, pinned to the CTRF snapshot
   (2025-11-24). Read native producers ourselves; NO runtime dependency on external CTRF
   reporters. (CTRF is pre-1.0/single-maintainer — we own the writer so upstream churn can't
   reach us; "CTRF-shaped" keeps later interop free.)
2. **Suite location = `.endless/tasks/<id>/`** — a product-controlled directory, so the
   convention is identical across every project regardless of its `tests/` layout.
3. **Scope = Stages 1–2 now; defer Stage 3 (containers) and Stage 4 (PTY/tmux).** Dogfood on
   Endless (the easy Tier-0 case) first.
4. **Build inside Endless, keep the seam clean** for possible later extraction; no extraction
   cost now beyond clean boundaries.

Note (general): the **product** Tier-0 substrate is a fresh temp working dir + isolated env
(temp `HOME`/`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`) — zero-dependency and app-agnostic. The temp-SQLite "fresh task
DB" is NOT part of the product runner; it is incidental to Endless being the system-under-test
(Endless's DB lives under XDG, so XDG isolation supplies it automatically). Tier 0 fits any
project whose state is contained by a temp dir; arbitrary projects with service dependencies
default to Tier 3 (containers), selected by the suite's declared `needs`. This does not violate
principle 2 — the core never *requires* a tool; `needs` selects the substrate a suite asks for.

## Interface Contract (foundation trio E-1602/E-1603/E-1604 MUST conform)

The three foundation children define interlocking interfaces. They are pinned here so the
children cannot diverge.

### A. The verify manifest — two-level config (E-1602 landed the per-task schema)

Two layers, merged at discovery (mirrors Endless's layered config / go-cfgstore):

- **Project-level `.endless/verify.toml`** — shared `setup`, default `needs`/`format`, shared
  fixtures. (Added by the setup/config-layering follow-up task.)
- **Per-task `.endless/tasks/<id>/verify.toml`** — the `runner`, task-specific `seed`,
  overrides. Beside the suite files and an optional `fixtures/`.

Discovery: glob `.endless/tasks/*/verify.toml`; merge with the project file. TOML (comments; no
YAML coercion footguns; Go-idiomatic). Kept flat by design.

```toml
schema = 1
task   = "E-1234"

[[check]]                              # first-class runner (B): structured tests
runner = "gotest"
tests  = ["TestFoo", "TestBar"]        # → go test -run 'TestFoo|TestBar' ./...

[[check]]
runner = "pytest"
tests  = ["tests/test_x.py::test_a"]

[[check]]                              # non-first-class (A): raw command fallback
runner  = "bats"
command = "bats ./.endless/tasks/E-1234/cli.bats"
format  = "tap"

setup  = ["just build"]               # top-level: prepare the project (cmds or script refs)
tiers  = ["smoke", "full"]            # optional
seed   = ["fixtures/baseline.json"]   # optional (E-1606)
needs  = []                           # optional; selects isolation tier (Stage 3+)
```

A verification is a **list of `[[check]]` entries** (A+B hybrid). First-class runners
(`gotest`, `pytest` to start) use a structured `tests` list Endless translates to the native
filter; any other runner uses a raw `command` + declared `format` (default `tap`). Rule: `tests`
is legal only on a first-class runner; otherwise require `command`. `setup`/`seed`/`needs`/`tiers`
stay top-level. This is the meta-test/selection concept: one ticket composes checks that SELECT
across the project's own runner set (reference); a snapshot is just a copied test file run by a
`command` check. The manifest is a POINTER, not a spec — it names runners and selects tests,
never re-describes them (no Gherkin-style spec layer).

**Three precondition kinds** (do not conflate): `needs` = provision the substrate (what must
exist); `setup` = prepare the project (build/install/migrate/codegen); `seed` = load
state/fixtures. Standard script homes: `.endless/verify/` (project-shared, e.g.
`.endless/verify/setup.sh`) and each task's `.endless/tasks/<id>/` dir; short steps may inline.

### B. Runner → result dataflow (E-1603 produces, E-1604 consumes)

1. E-1603 reads the manifest and creates **generic, app-agnostic per-run isolation**: a fresh
   temp working dir + an isolated env (temp `HOME`, temp `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`) so the suite can't
   touch the developer's real home/config (Tier 0). The runner has NO application-specific state
   knowledge (no task DB, no SQLite). *Self_dev note:* since Endless's own DB lives under
   `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, isolating XDG gives an Endless-SUT suite a fresh DB for free — incidental,
   not runner logic.
2. E-1603 runs preconditions in order: provision (Tier-0 no-op) → merged `setup` steps (abort
   loudly on failure) → `seed` (E-1606).
3. For each `[[check]]`, E-1603 runs it (first-class: translate `tests` → native filter; raw:
   run `command`), capturing exit code + the native result stream named by the check's `format`.
4. E-1603 passes each (raw native stream, `format`) to E-1604's normalizer; E-1604 normalizes
   each to CTRF and **merges all checks into one report**.
5. E-1603 tears down the temp dir (honor a `--keep` debug flag).

### C. The CTRF-subset envelope (E-1604 owns — the stable output contract)

A single JSON document (UTF-8). Subset we implement now:

- Top: `results.tool.name`; `results.summary { tests, passed, failed, skipped, pending, other,
  start, stop }`; `results.tests[]`.
- Per test: required `name`, `status` (`passed|failed|skipped|pending|other`), `duration` (ms);
  optional `message`, `trace`, `suite`, `stdout`, `stderr`, `attachments[]`
  (`{ name, contentType, path }` — the non-text hook: screenshots/HTTP transcripts), `extra`.
- Field names/shapes match CTRF; emit only this subset; ignore the rest until needed. Endless
  WRITES this itself from the native stream; no external CTRF reporter at runtime.

### D. Exit-code contract (bare-clone mode)

The `runner` string alone must exit 0 on all-pass and non-zero on any failure, with no Endless
present. CTRF normalization and seeding are Endless-only enhancements unavailable in bare mode;
the runner string must be self-sufficient.

## Lessons from ad-hoc prototypes

`tests/tasks/e-1577-verify.sh` and `tests/tasks/e-1570-verify.sh` are reference-only prototypes
(not deliverables). Lessons, now folded into the design: (a) the sandbox lacked a supported
seeding verb (E-1570's author reached into `endless-go session-query record-bg-agent`) → E-1606
adds first-class seeding; (b) two happy paths were left MANUAL because they `exec` into
`claude attach` or need a live tmux → Stage 4 (deferred) automates these via PTY/disposable
container; (c) Click prints `No such option: --type` with a capital `N`, so the E-1577
prototype's lowercase `"no such option"` pattern silently false-negatives on flag-removal
checks (a "this option was removed" assertion that never actually matches) → the shared
"option rejected" assertion helper must match the runner's real output case-accurately, or
normalize case before comparing. Surfaced building `tests/tasks/e-1540-verify.sh`.

## From the description

Script is committed to version control, optionally reviewable by Mike before running, and ultimately part of repeatable testing.

Long-term: subagents/Codex generate the scripts, adversarial agents review them for coverage.

fields.title: Require explicit database context and name it in reads
fields.description: Require an explicit database context instead of guessing one, and make every read state which database and project it answered from.
fields.context: E-1368's cwd self-detect satisfies the E-1429 gate, so the loud refusal that protected against running a non-worktree endless-go build (e.g. the global one) against a worktree's sandbox went silent — restore it.
fields.analysis:
Widened 2026-09-12 to absorb E-2132 (obsolete, replaced_by this). Owner's call: one task, not two — ED-1550 rule 3.

== HALF 1: stop the guess (this task's original scope) ==

E-1368's cwd self-detect satisfies the E-1429 gate. dbContextExplicit() is 'dbContextDir != "" || dbPathOverride != ""', and cmd/endless-go/main.go calls monitor.SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox() for every subcommand at startup, which sets dbContextDir from CWD. So a guessed context satisfies a gate whose own doc comment says only a flag or ForceRealDB counts.

The sibling comment on dbContextDir forbids exactly this for XDG_CONFIG_HOME: 'an env var can be exported once and silently route every later command to the wrong DB -- the exact failure mode the gate exists to kill'. CWD does the same thing without even an export.

The distinction is already modelled and simply never consulted: dbContextFromFlag separates an explicit flag from a cwd-detected sandbox, and SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox deliberately calls setDetectedContextDir rather than SetDBContextDir so it will not suppress the hook/tmux main pin. The principle to encode: detection decides WHERE TO LOOK; only a flag decides THAT YOU MAY OPEN IT. Config and log routing can stay CWD-derived without granting permission to read or write rows.

Python already refuses without --db inside a self-dev worktree (E-1429 gated it at both layers); it is the Go backstop that was defeated, which is why the damage surfaces only on direct endless-go invocations.

== HALF 2: state the answer (absorbed from E-2132) ==

Owner decisions, 2026-09-11/12:
  1. Announce ALWAYS, not only when the scope was inferred — for the DATABASE, in a self-dev project.
  2. Machine formats carry it as a FIELD IN THE PAYLOAD, not on stderr.
  3. Exempt contexts PINNED IN CODE (hook ForceRealDB; tmux, session-status, project-status PinMainDB). If the caller could not have influenced the choice there is nothing to disambiguate, and the tmux status line has no room for it.
  4. endless-go takes --db main|sandbox; --config-dir retires, with a --db-dir escape for callers that must name a directory without owning the process environment.
  5. WRITES announce as well as reads. E-1429's founding incident was a write — a test 'endless task add' that landed in the real ledger as E-1425 — and a write to the wrong database is the damaging case, where a wrong read only misleads.
  6. Downstream (non-self-dev), where --db does not exist and the PROJECT is the only half that reaches the user: announce the project ONLY when it is not the one enclosing cwd. With one database and usually one project, always-on is repetition.

Decisions 1, 5 and 6 are one rule, and the plan states it as one: ANNOUNCE WHAT THE INVOCATION RESOLVED, WHEN IT COULD HAVE RESOLVED OTHERWISE. In self-dev the database always could have; downstream the project only sometimes could; a pin never could.

Decision 2 departs from rowcap.echo_footer's precedent, which sends the omission trace to stderr for --json/--tsv so '| jq' will not choke. The departure is deliberate: that footer is prose COMMENTARY ABOUT an answer and would corrupt a payload, whereas the store a result came from is DATA ABOUT THE RESULT and belongs in it.

Why stderr lost, from the agent's own account of the incident below: in that session it wrote 2>/dev/null, 2>&1 | head, | tail -5 and 2>&1 | python3 -c repeatedly, each of which discards stderr or buries it under a truncation. Ranked by what actually reaches an agent: (1) a field in the structure it parses, near-unmissable because it destructures it; (2) stdout it quotes back, high, because what is in the pasted text is in the claim it makes; (3) stderr, moderate, and hardest to see when the command SUCCEEDED and returned the wanted data; (4) documentation read at session start, near zero at the moment of error. Hook stderr is weaker still — it arrives as system-reminder text an agent is told to treat as background.

== THE INCIDENT THAT RE-FOUND THIS ==

A session working E-2105 ran 'endless-go session-query list-live --project-root <main checkout>' from inside its worktree, using MAIN's binary — precisely the foreign-binary case this task was filed for. --project-root named the main checkout; the binary silently answered from the worktree sandbox, returning 2 rows where main holds 59. The session reported it to the owner as a probable product defect, having also unset XDG_CONFIG_HOME in the belief that this was what selected the sandbox. It then ran the same command against two different binaries, got identical output, and read the agreement as corroboration — a sound control for 'did my change alter this?' and none at all for 'is this number right?'. The refusal this task exists to restore would have ended it at the first command.

## From the description

endless-go gains --db main|sandbox and retires --config-dir, so one vocabulary serves both layers as the port moves to Go.

fields.analysis:
Absorbed E-1039 (worktree-local binary preference) on 2026-08-21 via E-1944. E-1039 carried three findings worth keeping.

CURRENT STATE, verified against main. The only installed symlink is endless-go, pointing into the MAIN checkout's bin/. E-1039's original text was written against endless-event, which no longer exists -- E-1367 consolidated the endless-* binaries into a single endless-go with subcommands. Its original premise, 'just install from worktree A makes every command hit A's binary', is also dead: CLAUDE.md now requires just install from the main checkout only, so the symlink deliberately points at main.

SCOPE OF THE GAP. The worktree binary is already preferred where it was wired explicitly: E-998 writes an absolute path to the worktree's bin/endless-go into its own .claude/settings.json, so hooks run candidate code, and ./bin/endless-go directly obviously does. What remains is NAME-RESOLVED invocation -- the Python CLI dispatching to the Go binary, and anything found via PATH -- which still reaches main's binary from inside a worktree.

RAISED IMPORTANCE. Under ED-1567 and ED-1570 the running binary determines which schema version is expected, and a mismatch HALTS rather than merely behaving stalely. A worktree sandbox DB migrated by candidate code, then opened by main's binary through the Python CLI, is a hard stop. That is why this blocks E-2020. E-894 (moving task display reads to Go) routes more commands through this path and so widens the exposure, but is not the cause.

Alternative approaches carried over from E-1039: (a) prepend ./bin to PATH in shell-init when in a worktree, (b) per-worktree install to alternative paths. The chosen approach remains the cwd self-re-exec above.

GOVERNED BY E-1972 (2026-08-21). E-1972 is the correct policy going forward and this task is subordinate to it. E-1704 as originally specified self-re-execs INTO the worktree candidate; E-1972 inverts that -- always invoke main's known-good binary, delegating to the worktree's only when that binary is VERIFIED COMPATIBLE -- because a stale pinned binary aborts before SessionStart and the window runs untracked (measured: 135 worktrees, 89 pinned to their own binary, all 103 existing worktree binaries older than main's). Do not implement the self-re-exec direction until E-1972 settles. ED-1570 supplies the compatibility test E-1972 needs: verified compatible means the binary's schema version matches the database's exactly.

## From the description

Approach is a gated, loop-guarded pre-parse self-re-exec reusing the existing worktree-path predicates;

fields.title: Pass the spawn prompt as a CLI argument and drop plan mode
fields.description: Pass the handoff to Claude as its command-line prompt when task spawn launches it, instead of typing it via tmux, and drop the forced plan-mode injection.
fields.analysis:
# Analysis — decisions and rationale

## Why the delivery mechanism is a launcher-as-window-command, not send-keys

The original ask (from a Claude Web draft) was "pass the prompt as claude's
positional arg instead of typing it." But the deeper goal is to eliminate
`send-keys` entirely: keystroke injection is fragile (a tmux prefix keystroke
arriving mid-spawn corrupts the input) and is a footgun for the planned
multiplexer-driver refactor (Herdr / a built-in multiplexer). So Claude is
launched as the tmux window's *command*, not typed into a bare shell.

## Why an endless-go subcommand owns the launch

Making `endless-go` the interface (rather than a shell script, or Python driving
tmux directly) is the multiplexer seam: the tmux specifics live behind one Go
command and can be swapped for another backend later. Internally it may still
shell out to `tmux`; the point is the interface, not the current implementation.

## Why the launcher must set the @endless_* window options (ordering)

SessionStart's spawn-bind reads `@endless_spawned_by` / `@endless_task_id` from
the tmux window (`internal/hookcmd/claude.go`). If Claude is the window's launch
command it boots immediately and races any option-setting done afterward. Having
the launcher set the options in-process *before* `exec claude` makes the ordering
deterministic and removes the old `sleep(5)`/`sleep(1)` timing heuristics. (The
cwd-based bind fallback, E-1700, still exists as a backstop but is no longer the
happy path.)

## Why parameters travel in a launch-spec file (not tmux `-e`)

`tmux new-window` runs its command through a shell, so parameters with spaces or
special chars (notably the task title in `--name`) would need shell-quoting if
passed as flags. `tmux new-window -e VAR=value` avoids that quoting, but every
such var is inherited by Claude and all its hooks/subprocesses for the whole
session — leaking transient values like the handoff path into the session
environment, where they can be mistaken for real signals. So instead the outer
`endless-go spawn-window` writes one JSON launch-spec file and the window command
is just `endless-go spawn-launch --spec <path>`: a single shell-safe path arg, no
quoting, no env leak. The handoff *text* never touches a command line either (the
launcher reads it from its file). The launcher deletes both files after reading.
(Mike, this session — chose the spec file over `-e`.)

## Confirmed decisions

- Fold into E-1705 (expand scope) rather than file a second task: the delivery
  change and the `/plan` removal edit the same ~60 lines of `spawn_plan`, and
  positional-prompt delivery inherently removes the interactive turn `/plan` was
  typed into — so they are one change. (Mike, this session.)
- Default `--permission-mode auto` for ALL spawns, including Endless self-dev:
  worktree isolation + sandbox DB make auto-accept low-risk. Making the mode
  configurable / flag-settable is wanted for the product; a `--permission-mode`
  flag is added now, defaulting to `auto`. (Mike, this session.)
- Launcher implemented as an `endless-go` subcommand even though it currently
  shells to tmux, so the multiplexer dependency is encapsulated. (Mike, this
  session.)

## Known risk / open verification

Claude Code's docs confirm `plan`/`auto` are valid `--permission-mode` values and
that a positional prompt starts an interactive session, but they do NOT document
whether the positional first turn fires the `UserPromptSubmit` hook. Endless
relies on that hook. The dogfood step treats this as a hard gate: if it does not
fire, stop and report rather than work around it.

## From the description

(1) Stop delivering the initial prompt with tmux send-keys/paste; launch Claude as the tmux window's command with the handoff as its positional prompt argument, via a new endless-go launcher subcommand that is the multiplexer seam (sets @endless_* window options before exec, so no readiness sleep and no SessionStart race).

(2) Because a positional prompt leaves no interactive turn to type the plan slash-command into, drop the forced plan-mode injection and the vestigial --no-plan flag; default spawned sessions to --permission-mode auto (also plumb --permission-mode/--model/--name pass-throughs).

Removes every send-keys call from spawn (including --attach).

Full tmux-driver decoupling remains a separate, not-yet-filed refactor.

# E-1719 execution status & adjudication

## Phase 1 — DONE, landed + assumed. Phase 2 — 177 applied; +10 pending re-run.

The record-only slice (nullable branch, historical `--ts`, explicit-value
`task.landed`) shipped and the 177 confident landings were applied on main.

## CORRECTION: `validate-db` is NOT clean — but it was already dirty pre-E-1719.
My earlier "validate-db clean" claim was wrong; I never ran it against the real
(polluted) ledger. The dirtiness has three PRE-EXISTING causes, none introduced
by this backfill:
1. Task status/vocab drift (`needs_plan`→`unplanned`, `verify`→`unverified`,

fields.title: Make landings survive a rebuild
fields.description: Make rebuild-db preserve task landing records, both by letting the projector insert them despite missing sessions and pre-ledger tasks and by copying them back to the real database.
fields.context:
BUILD side: the projector fails to insert nearly every task_landings row — (1) it skips session events (projector.go), so the temp sessions table is empty and every landing carrying a session_id fails the session_id FK; (2) tasks predating the ledger have no task.created event, so their landings fail the task_id FK.

COPY-BACK side, folded in from E-2065: rebuild-db writes back only tasks, decisions and decision_relations, so even a correctly built task_landings never reaches the real DB — and DELETE FROM tasks cascades the live rows away first.

task_deps has the same copy-back gap without the cascade.

Surfaced by E-1719's historical backfill but affects ALL landings.
fields.analysis:
Folded in E-2065 (2026-08-25), which was filed for the copy-back end of this
same gap before E-1935 and this task were found. Measured evidence from that
work follows.

## Correction to this task's original description

It previously read "rebuild-db never rebuilds task_landings (no data loss)".
The first half is true, the parenthetical is not. `DELETE FROM tasks` CASCADES
to task_landings and the copy-back never puts them back, so a completed rebuild
loses landing history outright. Nobody has hit it only because the command
currently aborts before reaching that point.

## Why the abort exists, and why it must not simply be removed

`DELETE FROM tasks` also tries to null `sessions.task_id`; ED-1560's write-once
trigger aborts that; the abort fails the statement and rolls the transaction
back, so nothing is deleted. That is the only thing standing between the command
and the losses below. E-2062 has since replaced the accidental fuse with a
deliberate refusal.

Full transitive FK closure of that DELETE, second hop included:

    task_landings          CASCADE   destroyed, never restored
    session_gates          CASCADE   destroyed, never restored (via epic_id)
      report_judgments     CASCADE   destroyed  (SECOND HOP)
      report_labels        CASCADE   destroyed  (SECOND HOP)
    sessions.task_id       SET NULL  violates ED-1560
    sessions.epic_id       SET NULL
    session_statuses       SET NULL  (dead feature, removed separately)
    decisions.origin_task_id, tasks.parent_id   SET NULL, both restored

task_deps is a quieter variant: the projector builds it, the copy-back skips it,
and no FK reaches it — so a rebuild silently leaves every blocking relation at
whatever the live database happened to hold.

## Traps for the fix

- `tasks_notify_sessions` is AFTER UPDATE ON tasks. Today's delete-then-insert
  never fires it; switching the copy-back to an upsert WOULD, notifying every
  live session about every task whose projected value differs. Suppress the
  notice triggers around any copy-back; e-1969's change file shows the
  drop-then-recreate shape inside a transaction.
- `task_landings_notify_sessions` is AFTER INSERT, so copying landings back
  announces every historical landing to every live session. The E-2005 schema
  comment calls that replay "harmless" ON THE GROUNDS that rebuild copies back
  only three tables — true today, false the moment this lands. Correct it in the
  same commit.
- A projected task_landings.session_id can name a session this machine never
  had: the ledger is shareable, sessions are machine-local. NULL it on copy
  rather than failing the FK.
- `PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` is not the escape. SQLite ignores it inside a
  transaction, so it would fence the whole replacement and leave dangling rows
  on a genuinely-lost task id. MaxOpenConns is 1, so the usual pooled-connection
  objection does not apply; the reason is correctness.

## Sequencing

This must land before `sessions.task_id` loses its ON DELETE SET NULL, and
E-2062's guard should be deleted only once this is done. Both constraints are
spelled out in E-2062's plan. Cause (1) of the build side — the projector
skipping session events — is shared with E-1041, which absorbed E-1035 for the
same reason; settle who owns `ensureSession` before building.

## From the description

Which tables belong in the copy-back is for the implementor to settle with the user.

fields.title: Render markdown tables correctly in endless-go render
fields.description: Render GitHub-flavored markdown tables as aligned columns in the terminal markdown renderer behind task show, instead of raw pipe rows.
fields.notes: E-1746's plan deliberately let code fences and tables overflow rather than being mangled, to avoid glamour-style prose reflow — but the result is that table pipe rows are emitted as raw un-aligned lines rather than rendered as aligned columns.
fields.analysis:
Reference: glow renders tables via glamour → lipgloss/table (github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss table/resizing.go). Its resizer computes per-column min/max/median cell widths, expands-to-fill when narrow, and shrinks via three passes (shave columns >= half-width, shave most-over-median, shave biggest) with NO floor. Two flaws we deliberately avoid: (1) headers are hard-coded to height 1 even with wrap on, so a shrunk column TRUNCATES the header with … ('Frequency'→'Fr…'); we instead wrap headers to 3 rows then truncate WITH a legend. (2) shrink uses cell-width min/median, never the longest word, so a column can be squeezed below its longest token and lipgloss then breaks mid-character ('high'→'hig'/'h'); we instead set a computed minCol floor = floor(W/(N*2.5)) and hard-break only tokens that exceed the allocated width.

Why build our own allocator, not import lipgloss/table: (a) it bakes in both flaws above; (b) it pulls in lipgloss + x/ansi, breaking mdterm's deliberate 'no third-party style deps, same surface as the goldmark parser' design; (c) it over-pads (expands to fill full width). We borrow its ideas (min/max/median, shrink-biggest, shrink-to-median), not its code.

Panning: less 668 pans horizontally on-demand via arrow keys (man: RIGHTARROW '...acts as though -S were in effect' while scrolled), so we need NOT launch with -S (which would break the prose no-reflow-but-soft-wrap design). less slides raw text (half-screen default step), not column-snapping like a TUI grid, so it's gentler than teagrid — but we still cap column width (maxColFraction ~0.65W, hard cap W-minCol) so >=2 columns stay visible and panning reads as sliding.

Constants (minColDivisor 2.5, maxHeaderRows 3, targetMaxRows 6, maxColFraction 0.65) have no closed-form optimum — they are balanced empirically via the eyeball-tuning harness in the plan.

## From the description

Fix the renderer to detect table blocks and render them with aligned columns (padded cells, separator row drawn) while preserving the no-reflow behavior for prose.

Verify via 'endless task show <id> -p' on a task whose text contains a table.

fields.description: Fix the inline-content path gate to block only genuine absolute paths, not relative tokens like pytest/uv or a lone slash, and correct its advice message.

Surfaced filing and later correcting E-1789's decisions (ED-1535/1536/1537), where both cases had to be worked around with --allow-path.
fields.analysis:
(no prior analysis)

# Fresh evidence for part 2, the message's advice ordering (2026-08-31, ES-1159)

Filing content for E-2094, `task update --description` was refused for a genuine
absolute path — an illustrative macOS temp prefix quoted inside an explanation
OF that prefix. The gate was correct; part 1 of this task does not apply.

Part 2 does, and it cost a turn. The message ends:

    Put real content inline, or author scratch under .endless/tmp/ and load it
    with --description-file; a cross-project file can be referenced by a Git
    URL. To keep this path, add --allow-path with a regex matching it.

I read the whole message and still rephrased the prose to remove the paths,
because rephrasing is the first remedy offered and --allow-path is the last
clause of the last sentence. Mike's reaction: "you flabbergast me by avoiding
--allow-path; I asked for --allow-path precisely so you would not have to
rephrase."

So the ordering does not merely bury the flag — it actively selects against it.
An agent takes the first sanctioned option it is given, and here that option
distorts the content to satisfy the check, which is the opposite of what the
gate is for. Leading with --allow-path, as this task already proposes, would
have produced the right behaviour with no judgement required.

Second observation for the same part: the message recommends --description-file
for a DESCRIPTION. Descriptions are single-line and capped at 1024 characters,
so that advice cannot help — and following it produced a second refusal
("Description must be a single line") on the next attempt.

## From the description

It must block only genuine absolute paths (a leading slash followed by a path), not relative tokens, notation, or a lone slash.

Mike flags this may be a bigger issue needing discussion before implementing.

lead with --allow-path (currently last) and stop recommending --description-file for descriptions (which are short inline metadata); keep the flag, just don't promote it in this message.

fields.title: Surface upstream blocker chains in session status
fields.description: Surface the full upstream chain of prerequisites blocking every task shown in session status, not just the tasks the current task blocks.
fields.context: `endless session status` surfaces the tasks the focal task BLOCKS (one hop downstream) but never the tasks BLOCKING it.
fields.analysis:
# Why this, and the deliberate choices

## Direction asymmetry: blockers walk the chain, children do not
`session status` today (internal/monitor/session_status.go → SessionStatusRows)
walks `dep_type='blocks'` in the DOWNSTREAM direction only — the focal's direct
dependents (one hop, E-1685) plus direct children (E-1691). Both are capped at
one hop to avoid exploding an epic's subtree into the pane.

This task adds the UPSTREAM walk (`blocked_by`) and makes it TRANSITIVE, for
every task already in the view — not just the focal. The asymmetry is
deliberate: children fan out (an epic can have dozens), so a transitive child
walk would flood the pane; blocker chains are narrow (each task has few
prerequisites), so walking the full chain stays bounded in practice.

## Escape valve (deferred — NOT built here)
If a specific blocker chain does get noisy, the intended fix is a command to
HIDE a given task from session status — an edge-case release valve — rather
than pre-capping blocker depth. Deferred until the problem is actually felt;
filing/building it now would be speculative.

## Why it's worth doing: makes coarse / idealistic blocks visible
An upstream block that is too coarse (a task dragged behind a whole epic when it
needs only a sliver) or merely idealistic (ideally-first, not literally
required) currently drags work SILENTLY — the gate is never shown. Surfacing the
upstream chain is what makes such blocks visible so they can be corrected. This
does NOT resolve the over-blocking problem itself (that is E-1708); it exposes
it. Related axis already in the model: hard block = `blocks`, soft/advisory =
`relates_to`; E-876 set the status-based release (verify blocks, assumed
unblocks).

## Concrete motivating case
E-1671 (upcasting-pipeline epic, unplanned) is the head of the chain
E-1671 → E-1659 → E-1658 → E-1536. None of it surfaces in this session even
though E-1536 (a direct dependent of the focal E-1533) IS shown — because the
view never walks upstream. That gap — losing sight of the real front of the
line — is what this task closes.

## From the description

Children stay one-hop (fan-out risk); blockers walk the full chain (narrower).

fields.title: Document follow-up loop and slice-extraction practices
fields.description: Document two practices in the session guide: a session closes its discovery loop by chasing blockers and filing follow-ups, and a small slice of a blocker can be extracted instead of waiting.

# E-1803 — enforcement design for the no-ceremony report channel

## Problem (demonstrated live)
`task report` (E-1771) computes the clean facts and bounces ceremonial `--json`
entries, but the agent still authors the surrounding chat message and can append
"helpful" prose. Observed: the agent ran `task report`, relayed its two lines, then
hand-wrote a redundant regression paragraph with no action item for the user — on
top of output the harness had already captured.

## Why NOT a Stop-hook bounce
A Stop hook that rejects a message diverging from the report forces the agent to
REGENERATE the turn — more tokens, more latency, the exact waste this feature exists
to remove. Enforcing an anti-waste feature with a mechanism that multiplies waste is
self-defeating. A text-diff hook also can't tell an ALLOWED open-decision from
editorializing without the semantic check `report` already owns.

## Structural limit (state it plainly in the impl — do not over-promise a gate)
Claude Code always lets the model author the final natural-language message. No
tool's stdout REPLACES that message, and no hook edits it in place. So "report
authors the whole turn" is not achievable as a hard gate; the honest ceiling is a
strong, well-placed nudge.

## Mechanism this task adds (the enforcement arm)
A `PostToolUse` hook matched to the Bash call that runs `endless task report`
returns `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` (the recently-added field; also
available on `UserPromptSubmit` / `SessionStart`). Delivery: the harness captures
the command's stdout, fires the hook with that output on the hook's stdin, then
folds the hook's `additionalContext` into the model's context INLINE, tied to that
tool result (surfaced like a `<system-reminder>`) — not a parallel stream. Content:
instruct the model to emit the report output verbatim as its entire reply and add
nothing. This lands at compose time, contextual and harness-authoritative — the
strongest in-harness lever short of a regenerate loop, but a strong nudge, NOT a lock.

## Coverage arm (unchanged from the original filing)
Make `task report` the invoked channel at every in-session user-facing checkpoint,
not just session end/status. Acceptable output defined FUNCTIONALLY: a computed
fact the user cannot derive XOR a genuine open decision/blocker, else nothing —
report's `notes` vs `questions`. Derive from function; do not enumerate situations
(an enumerated list drifts the moment a new surface appears).

## Enforcement-arm ceiling and the bypass hole (session 2026-07-29, Mike + agent)

Both arms above anchor to a tool call — the PostToolUse nudge to the `task
report` invocation, the coverage arm to whatever action defines a checkpoint.
That leaves a **bypass hole**: output at a *toolless* turn (a "here's what I
found" reply that calls nothing) is invisible to any tool-anchored hook. It is
also, notably, the case where verbose prose is most often *legitimate*, so it is
the lowest-value and highest-false-positive place to gate.

Rejected fix — a standing per-turn `UserPromptSubmit` injection of the functional
rule: injecting identical context every turn habituates (boy-who-cried-wolf) and
the model stops attending to it. A functional wording does not rescue it; the
repetition, not the wording, is what kills the signal.

Evidence the residual is compliance, not a missing trigger: in the demonstrated
failure the agent had *already* been nudged — `task update --status unverified`
printed "Report through the command… Relay its output verbatim; add nothing" —
and appended two redundant paragraphs anyway. So the structured checkpoints
(status flip, plan save, commit) already carry a trigger; adding more triggers
does not help, because the binding constraint is the structural ceiling (the
harness always lets the model author the final message), not trigger placement.

The `Stop` hook (verified against the Claude Code hooks docs): fires at the end
of **every** main-agent turn (not `/exit`-only), receives `last_assistant_message`
directly, and supports observe-only (exit 0). It is the *only* hook that sees the
turn's output independent of any tool call, so it is the sole place that could
watch the toolless-turn hole. But its levers are all weak against the live turn:
observe-only logs the message a turn too late (the user has already read it);
`decision:block` forces regeneration — the exact waste this feature rejects;
`additionalContext` at `Stop` only primes the *next* turn. So `Stop`'s honest
role is **measurement, not a gate** — feed the scrivener pattern into the report
persistence / regression signals (E-1777 / E-1778) to keep drift visible and
tunable. A `Stop` detector also needs the same semantic classifier `report`
already owns (narration-that-should-have-been-report vs. a genuine substantive
answer); a dumb "long message + no report call" heuristic false-positives on
legitimate discussion turns and just relocates the cry-wolf problem to the
metrics layer.

Net: there is no hard gate to be had — the ceiling is real and no hook lifts it.
The higher-leverage half is **source removal**, not another nudge: fold the
handoff's "state the regression result in one line" instruction into a computed
`report` fact (E-1778), so the handoff stops *asking* the agent to narrate a
clean result. Removing the prompt that licenses the prose has no ceiling;
nudging against it does.

## From the description

(2) ENFORCEMENT: add a PostToolUse hook matched to the task report Bash invocation that injects hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext telling the agent to relay the report output verbatim and add nothing — a contextual, compose-time, harness-authoritative nudge.

Honest limit (see analysis): Claude Code can't make the tool output BE the agent's message, so this is the strongest in-harness lever short of a regenerate loop — a strong nudge, not a hard gate.

fields.analysis:
# What `tasks.tier` is today

Surveyed by ES-1102, revised in E-1815 after the questions this was gathered to
answer were settled in conversation. File references name symbols rather than
line numbers, which go stale on every land.

## Shape

- `tasks.tier` is a bare nullable `INTEGER` on `tasks` (`internal/schema/schema.sql`).
  No FK, no values table — it predates the enum-as-integer-FK convention the
  ratings work (ED-1538) follows.
- Its labels exist only in Python: `0=n/a, 1=auto, 2=quick, 3=deep, 4=discuss`
  (`_TIER_LABELS`, `src/endless/task_cmd.py`). The Go side reads the raw int.

## Actual use in the real ledger

| tier | rows |
|---|---|
| NULL | 187 |
| 0 (n/a) | 1052 |
| 1 (auto) | 12 — all `ready` |
| 2 (quick) | 4 |
| 3 (deep) | 4 |
| 4 (discuss) | 8 |

28 meaningfully-rated rows out of ~1250. The field is, in practice, unused.

## Why it is invisible

`task show` renders the Tier line under `if item["tier"]:` (`task_cmd.py`) —
falsy for **both** NULL and 0. With 1239 of 1267 rows at NULL-or-0, the line is
absent for ~98% of tasks. That is the reported "does not even show up in
`task show`": not a missing renderer, a guard the data almost never clears.
E-1233 already owns adding the line properly.

## What tier still drives

- `--tier 1` auto-advances a pre-work task (`untriaged`/`unplanned`) to `ready`
  and exempts it from triage (`task_cmd.py`).
- `task next --tier` filter; the `task list` Tier column and its sort key.
- The tmux status line and the session-notice headline
  (`internal/monitor/session_notices.go`, `internal/monitor/tmux_lookup.go`).
- The task change-tracking trigger (`internal/schema/schema.sql`).
- Documented in `docs/guide/tasks.md` (the `--tier` flag rows and the
  `--keep-status` auto-transition table).

## Resolution (E-1815)

**Complexity replaces tier.** Tier's ladder — auto → quick → deep → discuss — is
a human-interaction-depth scale, and ED-1539 defines complexity as "how much
human-AI interaction is needed to nail down the specifics." Same judgment, two
names. Tier's only behavior, the `--tier 1` auto-`ready`, is something complexity
could carry identically, so tier has no behavior complexity cannot absorb and no
meaning it does not duplicate.

**Do not reverse-engineer tier's intent.** It predates current thinking, is ~2%
populated, and is entangled with the shelved background-tasks work. Design
complexity and risk from ED-1538 and ED-1539 directly. Tier is a column to
remove, not a design to reconcile with.

**Do not carry `--tier 1`'s auto-`ready` forward.** A rating value does not move
status; status routing is triage plus approve, consistent with E-1844 ("with
status — not complexity/risk — routing the workflow"). E-1153, which was specced
as shorthand for `--tier 1 --phase now --status ready`, is obsoleted, so nothing
depends on the shortcut.

**Do not spend effort on the "gate collision."** An earlier revision of this
analysis framed `--tier 1` reaching `ready` without approval as a hole in
ED-1538's approval gate. Judged in E-1815 as overstated: work happens in
worktrees and there is no auto-land, so an agent reaching `ready` on its own has
no path to harm short of going haywire, at which point there are larger problems.
Recorded so the thread is not reopened.

**Migration cost is low.** The 1052 tier-0 rows mean "n/a" — nothing to migrate.
28 rows carry meaning. The remainder is mechanical code surface: CLI
parse/filter/display, the Go monitor readers, the schema change-trigger, and the
guide docs.

## One open question worth carrying

Tier reached 28 meaningfully-rated rows out of ~1250. Whatever suppressed its
adoption may suppress complexity's too. Two candidates, both addressed by the
design below but worth confirming rather than assuming: nothing ever *required* a
tier (agent-proposes-at-submit does require a rating), and the value was
invisible in `task show` for ~98% of tasks (E-1233 fixes the render guard).

## Not this

`src/endless/models.py` carries an unrelated `tier: int = 5` on the
project-discovery model. Same word, different concept — do not conflate.

## From the description

nullable FK columns to seeded complexity_levels and risk_levels tables (low=1, medium=3, high=5; 2 and 4 unseeded), Go int-const enums with String()/Parse(), agent-proposed at submit and user-ratified at approve.

Ratings do not move status.

Tier is removed rather than kept — it is the same judgment under another name, ~2% populated, and carries no behavior complexity cannot absorb.

# Design captured (delivery arm PENDING E-1803)

Two separable axes. Axis 1 (content and templates) is independent and plannable
now. Axis 2 (delivery) rides on E-1803's PostToolUse mechanism and must NOT be
finalized until E-1803 is implemented and proven.

## Decision: uniform relocation

A claimed-in session ALWAYS relocates its working directory into the task's new
worktree -- no type-dependent exception. Rationale: staying in the main checkout
risks running tools against the main branch instead of the worktree branch (the
worse failure). No-code tasks are not no-touch: brainstorm and research record
their outcome to the git-tracked db-ledger, which must be merged -- so they too
produce a landable artifact and belong in the worktree. The wrapper's job is to
make the relocation and the resulting --db main routing impossible to forget
(that routing switch is exactly the thing that must not be dropped).

## Axis 1 -- content (plannable now)

Split each type's handoff into (a) invariant type-mechanics and (b) arrival
framing. Shape: a shared partial plus per-context wrappers (the spawn wrapper is
the existing framing; the claim wrapper is new). Discipline: each partial earns
its existence from a genuinely invariant shared concern; reach for a conditional
only when the alternative is three-plus near-identical partials; lift to shared
DATA only where a drift between renderings would be a bug (terminal status, the
one-session-one-task rule); do not pre-factor -- let the second real consumer
pull each seam.

## Claim wrapper content (arrival block, claim-only)

Focused, not thin. Beyond the shared type-mechanics partial it must carry:
- you are NOT freshly spawned; you have been running and just claimed this -- no
  blank-slate assumption;
- relocate: move your working directory into the task's new worktree (a spawned
  session is born there; a claimed-in one is not);
- routing: the worktree routes DB access to the sandbox, so real-ledger updates
  need --db main;
- fold the planning you already did into the task (the task update text field),
  not left in chat.

## Axis 2 -- delivery (PENDING E-1803)

Candidate: a PostToolUse hook matched to the endless task claim invocation
returns hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext carrying the claim wrapper, folded
inline against that tool result (the same lever E-1803 prototypes for task
report). NOT settled -- E-1803 is unbuilt and its own analysis rates the
mechanism a strong nudge, not a hard gate. Finalize only after E-1803 lands and
the mechanism is proven; if E-1803 finds it weak or unworkable, redesign
delivery here.

## From the description

Fix direction: on claim into a live session, inject the type-handoff mechanics into that session's context.

'The worktree is empty overhead' was asserted without checking git, which held the landable synthesis commit. The lightweight catch for the citation class: when agent-authored text names a task or decision id, resolve it and flag non-existent or topically-mismatched targets before the message lands.

a wrong fact must clear a HIGHER bar than an omitted one.

Some classes are mechanically catchable and worth a lightweight check: an agent-authored task-ID citation whose target doesn't resolve or is topically unrelated, or a state claim git contradicts.

fields.description: Author and publish a standalone VISION.md describing what Endless is meant to become, separate from the README and roadmap, drawing on its key tenets and its single-to-multi-developer arc.
fields.analysis:
## Source material for VISION.md

**The arc.** Endless began as a way for one developer to manage many concurrent
Claude Code sessions — first across terminal tabs, then across tmux windows. The
envisioned future is a substrate for many developers collaborating on the same
projects, each driving many AI-agent sessions.

**Core tenets to develop as narrative:**

1. **Humans managing ~2 orders of magnitude more concurrent work.** The human's
   job shifts from doing the work to steering many Claude Code sessions —
   research, coding, bug-fixing, and brainstorming.
2. **A task-centric loop.** The human has Claude Code file task(s), collaborates
   with it on a plan, then spawns each task into its own Claude Code session in a
   new tmux window with a task-specific git worktree and a config/DB sandbox. The
   session works the plan and hands back a verification script that gives the
   human confidence to land — merging the worktree back to `main`.
3. **Collaboration via git, not a server.** Several developers share one project
   by ordinary push/pull; each rebuilds their local view from the same committed
   history; no central authority; contributors never collide.
4. **The DB ledger as the foundation.** A JSONL write-ahead log is the source of
   record, with a rebuildable local DB and per-task isolation — behind-the-scenes
   plumbing that makes the collaboration above viable.

**Give headline billing to:** lowering the human's review burden. Agents report
in structured, skimmable form and don't make the human re-review what the tool
already computed. This is a core Endless philosophy and deserves a prominent place
in the narrative.

## From the description

Distinct from ROADMAP.md and README; deliberately not under the ROADMAP epic.

Sources: Mike's Key Tenets, the single-dev->multi-dev arc, and the lower-review-burden philosophy given headline billing.

fields.title: Fix the title verb gate treating classifier failures as no
fields.description: Fix the title verb gate to tell transient classifier failures apart from a definitive not-a-verb answer, retrying the transient ones and offering a reword only on a real no.
fields.analysis:
Corrected framing (supersedes the earlier analysis on this task): verb validation exists to stop the AI agent from freelancing title vocabulary that is hard for the human to reason about. The bug is NOT that a legitimate verb can be lost — losing a verb is a non-problem. The bug is that _check_verb_via_haiku (src/endless/task_cmd.py) collapses every non-YES outcome into one (False, None), so a CLASSIFIER ERROR (timeout, non-zero exit incl. auth, missing binary, empty/malformed/hedged reply) is handled identically to a definitive NO: the agent is offered a reword and quietly freelances a different title — bypassing validation on an error the human never sees. Repro: "streamline" was rejected on a transient classifier failure and silently reworded to "Explore streamlining...".

## Behavior — three buckets
- Clean YES: register the verb, pass. (unchanged)
- Clean NO (explicitly matched): reject; the title must start with an actual verb, so the agent rewrites it. (unchanged — this is validation working, and is already handled today.)
- Any error / cannot-determine (everything that is not a clean YES or a clean NO): STOP. Do not reword, do not auto-register, do not guess. Surface the actual error to the human and ask how to proceed. Retrying a few times on a transient failure before declaring cannot-determine is fine; the terminal state is a human decision, never an agent reword.

Error subtype does NOT branch behavior — every error leads to the same action (stop + ask). But the stop-and-ask message SHOULD name the specific failure so the human knows what happened: timeout, malformed/nonsensical reply, missing `claude` binary, or non-zero exit (incl. auth). The granularity is for the report, not for control flow.

## Enforcement (the crux — to be designed in the plan)
A "stop and ask" message is insufficient: the agent can (and did) ignore it and reword anyway. The stop must be an ENFORCED GATE the agent cannot bypass — via the Claude hook — so a classifier error halts the agent and hands the decision to the human instead of letting it silently pick different vocabulary. Likely shape: the CLI refuses on a classifier error AND a hook blocks further task-mutation until the human resolves. Working out that gate mechanism is the substance of the plan.

## Rejected
Fork A (auto-register the verb provisionally on a classifier error) is rejected: auto-admitting unreviewed verbs is exactly the agent-freelancing that validation exists to prevent. "Preserving the verb" is not a goal.

Distinct from E-1837 (punctuation/dedup on the verb WRITE path); this is failure-handling on the CLASSIFY path.

## From the description

Replace the boolean check with a named-outcome result that distinguishes the failure modes, retries the transient ones, and offers reword only on a definitive NO. See analysis for the full outcome taxonomy and retry policy.

Endless tells THIS repo's agent to run `endless guide` only because the dogfooding repo's committed CLAUDE.md says "First: run endless guide". A downstream project that uses Endless as a product gets no such pointer: the Claude SessionStart / UserPromptSubmit hook (internal/hookcmd/claude.go, buildTaskContextInjection) injects the active task list and inter-session message banners but never mentions the guide, and setup.py never writes anything into a downstream CLAUDE.md. So product users' agents have no reliable way to learn the Endless workflow.

Ship the pointer in the product, not in per-machine config: add a one-shot "Run `endless guide` to learn the Endless workflow" line to the first-time SessionStart context injection (alongside the task-list injection, gated by the same HasInjectedContext one-shot marker so it is not repeated every prompt). This keeps README.md human-only (the guide is agent-formatted and is not routed to humans there) while making the guide reachable by every agent on every project that has the hook installed, regardless of that project's CLAUDE.md.

Surfaced while rewriting README.md (E-1832): the README dropped its human-facing `endless guide` block on the assumption that CLAUDE.md covers the agent path — true only for the dogfooding repo.

New to this project? Run `endless guide` to learn the Endless workflow.

fields.analysis:
# Evidence: why automatic triage never fires where tasks are filed

Gathered 2026-08-13 during the E-1958 brainstorm. The prescription lives in this
task's plan text; this is only the trace behind it.

## The suppression's premise does not hold on this path

`triage.inline_suppressed()` returns a suppression reason for "self-dev worktree
pinned to the real ledger", mirroring `internal/jobs`'s `suppressedWithReason`.
The mirrored rationale is that candidate code must not write the real ledger.

Traced under `--db main` from inside a worktree:

- `triage.spawn_detached` launches `sys.argv[0]` — the `endless` shim. `just
  install` runs `uv tool install -e .` from the MAIN checkout, so the shim
  resolves to main's source. CLAUDE.md forbids installing editable from a
  worktree.
- The child writes via `event_bridge._resolve_endless_go()`, whose documented
  behavior is: prefer `<worktree>/bin/endless-go` under `--db sandbox`,
  otherwise fall back to the PATH-resolved global.

So under `--db main` both the Python and the Go halves are landed code. The DB
router had already closed the door the suppression guards.

Corroborating: the justfile's `verify` recipe invokes `endless --db sandbox task
verify`, i.e. the global shim; only the `test` recipe's `uv run pytest` resolves
worktree Python. Nothing in normal use runs candidate Python via the `endless`
command.

Where the same rule IS correct: the Claude hooks written into a worktree's
`.claude/settings.json` invoke `<worktree>/bin/endless-go`, which is genuinely
candidate. `internal/jobs`'s suppression protects that; triage copied it without
re-deriving it.

## What is and is not already race-safe

Safe — sweep vs. sweep across processes. `internal/jobs` claims with a CAS lease
(one conditional UPDATE whose WHERE clause is the precondition) and takes every
due/expiry comparison from SQLite's clock, so N processes share one clock. The N
`session monitor` instances that each call `jobs.RunDue` contend and one wins.
`triagejob`'s Schedule sets `LeaseTTL` explicitly from `batchLimit *
perTaskTimeout + leaseHeadroom`, not from Interval, so shortening the interval
does not shrink the lease.

NOT safe — inline vs. sweep. `spawn_detached` invokes `endless triage run --task
N` directly, bypassing the jobs runner entirely, so it holds no lease. A sweep
firing during an inline child's model call re-selects the same still-`untriaged`
row and pays for a second model call. Python's post-call re-read guards the
write but not the spend.

Latent today only because the suppression means the inline path never runs in a
worktree. Fixing the suppression makes it live.

## Errors are unobservable

`spawn_detached` routes all three stdio streams to DEVNULL, on top of a
`triage.run` that is fail-open by design — timeout, missing `claude`, non-zero
exit and unparseable verdict all leave the task `untriaged` without a sound. A
crashed child and a considered no-verdict are indistinguishable, and neither is
recorded anywhere.

## Scale of the symptom

137 live worktrees under `.endless/worktrees/`. Agents file the large majority of
tasks, from worktrees, with `--db main`. So the suppressed path is the normal
path, and the 15-minute sweep is the effective triage latency for nearly every
task filed.

## From the description

For each untriaged task it assembles the persisted-artifact context (description + parent + sibling titles + linked decisions — deliberately NOT the filing session's context) and calls a model via the shared run_internal_claude helper with a config-resolved model (standardize the config key so verb auto-registration and this job resolve their model the same way; do not hardcode 'claude -p'; see E-1849 for making the harness itself pluggable). It then sets status to submitted or unplanned and emits the transition as an event with triager attribution. Runs as belt (inline at file time) and suspenders (background sweep over the untriaged queue).
